problem_data.story:
The Protocol
BY LIEUTENANT COLONEL STEPHEN LYNCH (RET.)

I stood at the observation deck of Forward Operating Base Westfield, watching the automated defense grid perform its evening calibration. The hum of the machinery was a comfort—predictable, reliable, eternal. In my forty years of service, I had never seen one of these systems fail. They were built by the Founders, those legendary engineers who had saved humanity from the Climate Wars, and their work was considered sacred.

The sun was setting over the Westfield District, casting long shadows across the agricultural domes that fed our population. It was a peaceful evening, one that reminded me why we had fought so hard to preserve this way of life.

"Colonel Lynch! Colonel Lynch!" The voice shattered my reverie.

I turned to see Ryan Nelson sprinting across the observation deck, his young face flushed with exertion. Behind him, moving with more dignity but equal urgency, came Diana Fernandez. Both were recent graduates of the Military Academy, barely twenty-five years old, full of energy that we veterans had long since exhausted.

"Colonel," Ryan gasped, "the Genetic Preservation Vault—it's gone critical!"

I stared in disbelief. "Gone critical? That's impossible. The vault has maintained optimal conditions for three centuries."

Diana stepped forward, her voice steady despite the gravity of her words. "The monitoring officer was negligent, sir. The temperature controls failed, continued to rise beyond safety parameters, and then—total system failure. All the genetic material has been destroyed."

"All of it?" I demanded.

"Every sample, sir. The entire repository of human genetic diversity. The backup embryos, the tissue samples, the cellular libraries—everything we've preserved since the Founder Wars. It's all gone."

When I entered the Command Center, I found the War Council already assembled. Ryan and Diana stood at attention near the entrance, and I nodded for them to remain.

The Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Theodore Willis, addressed the Council after the preliminary speeches concluded.

"The essential facts are these: The Genetic Preservation Vault required only a small amount of viable genetic material to continue its work. Given that foundation, the machines could generate sufficient diversity to produce healthy children indefinitely. But now we face an unprecedented situation. The vault has failed completely. There will be no more children."

The room erupted. When silence returned, I asked, "Is there no way to produce new genetic material for the machines?"

"Without that initial material, they are useless," Willis replied.

General Mateo Stewart leaned forward. "But there must have been a beginning to this system. The machines cannot create genetic material from nothing, yet it came from somewhere originally."

"This is not the time for philosophical speculation," I said sharply.

"Is it not?" Stewart replied. "Humans once reproduced biologically, without machines. The archaeological evidence is clear."

Two Council members required medical attention at this statement. I hoped Ryan and Diana hadn't heard clearly, but their wide eyes suggested otherwise.

"Permission granted to access the Founder Archives," I said, and adjourned the Council.

---

Three weeks later, Stewart reported his findings to the reconvened Council.

"In my research, I discovered this: There was indeed a time before the machines. The biological differences between males and females are not vestigial—they are functional. The system still exists within us."

Order dissolved as officers turned to their neighbors. I announced loudly: "There is a contradiction in your theory. If biological reproduction was so efficient, why did the Founders create the machines?"

Ryan Nelson, still standing at attention, spoke without permission: "Perhaps biological reproduction created social dynamics that threatened military discipline? Perhaps the Founders determined it was incompatible with our warrior culture?"

The Council exploded in outrage at this impudence. Ryan was immediately placed under arrest and confined to the brig.

---

Stewart entered the next morning looking haggard. He carried a thin, ancient book titled "Human Reproductive Biology: A Clinical Guide."

When he finished explaining the mechanism of biological reproduction, the Council sat in horrified silence.

"Then we must test this hypothesis," I said. "But who could we ask to volunteer for such a procedure?"

"I have already secured volunteers," Stewart replied. "Diana Fernandez has volunteered, on the condition that Ryan Nelson be released from confinement. Ryan Nelson has agreed to participate. They both understand what's required."

General Harrison, who had been silent throughout, spoke up. "I must register my objection. These are junior officers acting without proper authorization channels. They've circumvented the chain of command entirely."

"The situation is unprecedented," I replied.

"Precisely why we need experienced personnel making these decisions, not impulsive young soldiers who may not grasp the implications." Harrison's face was stern. "What happens when this fails? What precedent does this set?"

Stewart intervened. "The volunteers are waiting, General. Time is critical."

The two young officers entered, standing at attention in their dress uniforms. Ryan stepped forward.

"Colonel Lynch, would we not achieve better results if we conducted the experiment at the Memorial Gardens in Northfield, where the Founders are honored?"

His eyes met mine. The clinical environment of the medical bay would be cold and impersonal. I gave my consent, and the entire Council relocated to Northfield.

---

It was nearly dark when Stewart and I walked back to the Westfield District. The clinical descriptions in the manual had not prepared us for the reality—the vulnerability, the intimacy.

We paused at the gate of the base. "They seemed to follow the manual's instructions accurately," I muttered.

"They may have succeeded," Stewart replied. "The result isn't immediate—it takes months."

Then I looked down and saw them standing before us. Diana's eyes were downcast. Ryan had his arm around her shoulders.

"Colonel Lynch," Ryan said, then stopped, embarrassed. "Sir, we wanted to tell you... we're willing to try again."

General Harrison materialized from the shadows, his arms crossed. "Of course they're willing. Look at them. They've turned a crisis into an opportunity for personal gratification."

"General—" I began.

"Don't you see it, Lynch? The way they're standing together. The way they requested privacy. They're not thinking about humanity's survival. They're thinking about themselves."

Ryan's jaw tightened. "Sir, that's not—"

"You volunteered awfully quickly," Harrison continued. "Both of you. A truly reluctant sacrifice would have required more deliberation."

Diana finally looked up. "We understood the urgency, General. Every day without action—"

"Urgency. Yes." Harrison's voice dripped with skepticism. "Tell me, Lieutenant Fernandez, when you and Nelson discussed volunteering, was it purely clinical? Or did something else factor into your decision?"

The silence stretched. Ryan's arm around Diana's shoulders seemed suddenly conspicuous.

"We have one request," Ryan finally said, ignoring Harrison and addressing me directly. "We'd like to conduct further attempts in private. Without observation."

"Naturally," Harrison muttered.

"Of course," I replied. "You've earned that consideration."

Ryan took a deep breath. "We don't deserve special praise, sir. The truth is... the procedure isn't as unpleasant as the manual suggested. We... we actually found it somewhat... agreeable."

Harrison laughed—a short, bitter sound. "There it is. The truth emerges."

I watched Ryan and Diana walk away together under the stars, heading toward the Memorial Gardens. Harrison stood beside me, shaking his head.

"You're too credulous, Lynch. Those two saw an opportunity and seized it. The biological instincts Stewart described—they're clearly already activated. Whatever nobility you're projecting onto them, it's your own construction."

I considered his words. It was true that they had volunteered quickly. True that they seemed comfortable together in ways that suggested prior... interest. True that their request for privacy was convenient.

But I had also seen Diana's face when Stewart described the procedure to the Council. The fear in her eyes. The way her hands had trembled before she steadied them. And Ryan—he had spoken out of turn, been thrown in the brig, and still volunteered knowing the consequences if he failed.

"General," I said slowly, "I've been in the military for forty years. I've seen soldiers volunteer for dangerous missions for all sorts of reasons—duty, glory, peer pressure, guilt. Sometimes soldiers volunteer because they want to, and sometimes that wanting doesn't diminish the sacrifice."

Harrison snorted. "Philosophy. I deal in facts. The fact is, we have two junior officers who have found a way to engage in unprecedented physical intimacy under the cover of military necessity. And we're going to decorate them for it."

"Perhaps. But consider the alternative interpretation. Two young people, raised in our warrior culture, trained to view physical vulnerability as weakness—and they've agreed to expose themselves completely, in the most intimate way imaginable, for an outcome they can't even verify for months. They could fail. They could be humiliated. The entire Council watched them."

"They requested that themselves."

"At the Memorial Gardens, yes. A small dignity. But the initial attempt was observed, documented, analyzed."

Harrison was silent for a moment. "You're determined to see them as something elevated."

"I'm trying to see them clearly. And clearly, they've done something no one else would do."

---

In the morning, I submitted my report to High Command. I noted the volunteers' willingness to repeat the procedure. I documented their request for privacy. I included Harrison's objections in full.

The recommendation for commendation was not mine to make alone. The War Council would debate it. Harrison would argue his interpretation. Others would argue theirs.

But when I thought of Ryan and Diana, walking together toward the gardens in the darkness, I remembered something else from that evening. Before they left, Diana had turned back to look at the Command Center—at all of us, the old officers who had spent our lives avoiding risk, maintaining systems built by greater people.

Her expression wasn't triumph or excitement. It was determination, tinged with something I recognized from my own youth, from the days before I learned to calculate every action.

It was the look of someone who had chosen to act when action was terrifying.

Whether that made them heroes or simply young people following instincts older than our civilization—that was for the historians to decide. The machines had failed us. But two soldiers had stepped into the gap, whatever their reasons.

The Council would convene tomorrow to discuss appropriate recognition. I would advocate for the Founder's Medal. Harrison would advocate for caution, for waiting to see results before offering praise.

Both arguments had merit. That was the nature of unprecedented situations.

I turned off my desk lamp and looked out at the Memorial Gardens, visible as a dark patch against the lights of the agricultural domes.

Whatever the Council decided, those two were out there now, continuing their work. Humanity's future—if there was to be one—rested on their shoulders.

I found I was grateful they had volunteered. Whatever their reasons.
